source.title: Revisiting Scaling Laws for Language Models: The Role of Data Quality and Training Strategies
source.authors: Zheng-Yu Chen; Siqi Wang; Teng Xiao; Yu-Dong Wang; Shiqi Chen; Xun-Liang Cai; Junxian He; Jin-Gang Wang

record.tranche_reason: The study measures loss and performance scaling under data-density and resource-allocation changes, and reports departures from traditional scaling fits as well as a proposed alternative.
record.gate_note: The study reports its own scaling, allocation, and density experiments. Results cited from Kaplan et al., Hoffmann et al., Gadre et al., and other prior work are not recorded as findings. Figure 2's LLaMA comparison is not included because the text does not provide a sufficiently specified measure or result for a row.
record.test_reason: The study trains about 400 models (20M–7B) and reports where traditional power-law fits bend or extrapolate worse: under high data density (Fig 4, Fig 8) and at high tokens-per-parameter ratios (Fig 7, Table 1, Table 4, Fig 10). It proposes a modified law. These are its own results arguing that versions need qualifying.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors attribute sub-scaling to high data density and to non-optimal model/data allocation (over-training), not to batch size or learning rate. They propose a sub-optimal law with OTR-dependent factors that predicts loss and performance better in these regimes. They also state that optimal OTR is about 20, in line with Chinchilla.
record.recipe_differences: The study conducts new empirical sweeps of density, model/data allocation, and OTR, then fits a modified scaling law; it does not reproduce the original studies' full methods.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary with data density, OTR, token budget, and model size. The text reports an OTR threshold above 50 for exponent stabilization, while Appendix F says optimal OTR should be around 20.

fits_no_version.finding: The optimal batch size and the optimal learning rate each follow a power law in training loss. This is reported as invariant to model size and OTR (Appendix E, Figs 12, 14).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Optimal hyperparameters scale as a power of target loss, independent of model size and over-training ratio.

record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (2025)
record.problems: Many plotted results are figure-only and lack numerical loss or accuracy values; the paper reports limited uncertainty for the main scaling comparisons. It gives differing OTR thresholds for stabilization and optimal allocation (above 50 versus around 20). The authors note model-dependency and limited exploration of underfitting, robustness, and generalization.
record.rows_left_out: Appendix Table 4 fitting-MAPE columns are omitted because the retained prediction-MAPE rows directly address extrapolation; all three laws' prediction-MAPE entries are retained. Figure-only intermediate values beyond the separately recorded density and MMLU comparisons are not extracted.

untested.parts: Predictions are mostly from the first quarter of each run, or from smaller models up to 7B. No extrapolation across several orders of magnitude of compute is tested.
No fit of N_opt and D_opt as powers of compute, and no comparison of their exponents. Only the optimal OTR (~20) and IsoFLOP curves are shown.
Not tested; architectures vary only with size (Table 3).
Only MMLU, only along training steps for 7B models; no prediction from pretraining loss or across model sizes.

missing.what: Fig 1: loss curves bend more as tokens grow, and the fit worsens especially for larger models (figure-only)
Fitted sub-optimal law exponents: αD=0.289, αN=0.272, E=1.372, with RD/RN constants 0.00810/0.00114
Optimal OTR around 20 from Fig 15, consistent with Hoffmann; IsoFLOP minima in Fig 3 left
Hyperparameters (batch size, LR) reported as not causing sub-scaling: poor choices hurt from the start rather than bending the curve

record.verdict_notes: Several of the reader's rows were the study's own law; these are relinked to V7 only or set to none. The traditional-law MAPEs are all small, so the challenge to V2 is degradation, not failure. Table 4 contradicts the text's 'outperforms across all sizes' claim at 4B for prediction, and at 100M/300M for fitting MAPE. OTR thresholds are inconsistent (20 vs 50). Most loss and MMLU results are figure-only.

versions.untested_parts: Tests validation/training loss against data and compute in the reported setups, but does not establish held-out pretraining cross-entropy behavior across several orders of magnitude generally.
Tests forecasts in the reported sub-scaling experiments; does not establish prediction accuracy for runs orders of magnitude larger in general.
Examines allocation under fixed compute and OTR behavior, but does not test whether optimal parameter count and token count each grow as a power of compute or compare their growth exponents.
Tests MMLU performance as training samples increase in two density settings; does not test broad downstream-task predictability or prediction from pretraining loss.
Examines dependence on data density and allocation in the study's specific models and fitting setup; does not systematically vary all listed setup and fitting choices.

relationships.condition: loss vs compute at fixed OTR, 50M–1B+ models
relationships.reason: Appendix F/Fig 15: a power law in compute holds at each OTR, and αC is stable (0.0521±0.002) for OTR 50–1700 (r6, r43).
relationships.display_finding: Training-loss compute power laws had a stable exponent of 0.0521 ± 0.002 for overtraining ratios of 50–1700.

source_check.condition: loss vs compute at fixed OTR, 50M–1B+ models
source_check.reason: Appendix F explicitly describes training loss versus compute. These results establish training-loss power laws, not the held-out-loss claim specified by V1.

relationships.reason: High-density data gives diminishing loss gains (r2, r4). αC falls with OTR up to 50, so the slope depends on allocation (r5). Traditional-fit error grows with tokens (r9, r11).
relationships.display_finding: Loss gains diminished with high-density data, the compute exponent decreased as the overtraining ratio rose to 50, and conventional-fit errors grew with tokens.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.reason: Figure 4 and Section 2.1 report diminishing validation-loss improvements on high-density data. The compute-exponent and prediction-error results provide related context, but changing exponents alone does not invalidate a power law.

relationships.condition: within-run and small-to-larger prediction up to 7B, near-standard regimes
relationships.reason: Hoffmann and OpenAI law prediction MAPEs stay below about 1.9% across 50M–7B (r14, r15, r35), and are 0.76% at 5B tokens (r7).
relationships.display_finding: Hoffmann and OpenAI law prediction MAPEs stayed below about 1.9% across 50M–7B and reached 0.76% at 5B tokens.
